subject: SCIENCE
chapter: Chapter 14 — Chemical Effects of Electric Current
name: Chemical Effects of Electric Current
summary: What a current does when it passes through a liquid instead of a wire.
source: NCERT Class 8 Science, syllabus topic coverage only
licence: Original questions written for EduLink · CC BY-SA 4.0

questions.stem: Which of these liquids is the best conductor of electricity?
choices: Lemon juice
Distilled water
Vegetable oil
Kerosene
questions.solution: Lemon juice contains citric acid, which splits into charged particles called ions when dissolved, and moving ions are what carry a current through a liquid. Distilled water, vegetable oil and kerosene contain almost no free ions, so they conduct very poorly or not at all.

questions.stem: What is the process of depositing a layer of one metal onto another using electricity called?
choices: Electroplating
Galvanisation by heating
Distillation
Sedimentation
questions.solution: Electroplating uses an electric current passed through a solution to deposit a thin coating of one metal onto the surface of another. It is used to make cheap metal look better, to resist rust, and to save expensive metal — a thin layer of silver on a steel spoon does the job of a solid silver one.

questions.stem: Why is distilled water a poor conductor of electricity while tap water conducts reasonably well?
choices: Distilled water has almost no dissolved salts, so it has almost no free ions to carry charge
Distilled water is colder than tap water
Distilled water contains no oxygen
Tap water is under higher pressure
questions.solution: Conduction in a liquid happens by ions moving, not by electrons as in a wire. Distillation removes the dissolved salts and minerals, and with them the ions. Tap water keeps those dissolved salts, so it conducts — which is exactly why it is dangerous to touch an electrical switch with wet hands, even though pure water by itself would be fairly safe.

questions.stem: A bulb fails to glow when testing whether a liquid conducts. What is the best conclusion to draw?
choices: The current may be too weak to light the bulb, so a more sensitive test such as a magnetic compass should be used
The liquid definitely does not conduct at all
The battery must be dead
The liquid must be an acid
questions.solution: A bulb needs a fairly large current before its filament glows visibly, so a weakly conducting liquid can pass a real current and still leave the bulb dark. Replacing the bulb with a compass needle placed near the wire is the standard fix — the needle deflects for currents far too small to light anything. Concluding 'no conduction' from a dark bulb is the reasoning error being tested.

questions.stem: In electroplating, to which terminal of the battery is the object being plated connected?
choices: The negative terminal, so it acts as the cathode
The positive terminal, so it acts as the anode
Either terminal — it makes no difference
Neither; it is left unconnected in the solution
questions.solution: The object to be plated is connected to the negative terminal and becomes the cathode. Metal ions in the solution carry a positive charge, so they are attracted to the negative electrode and deposit there. Connecting it the other way round would strip metal off the object rather than adding it, which is the same process running backwards.

questions.stem: Why are the taps and handlebars of bicycles often coated with chromium?
choices: Chromium resists corrosion and scratching and keeps a shine, while the cheaper metal underneath provides the strength
Chromium is lighter than every other metal
Chromium conducts electricity better than steel
Chromium is cheaper than iron and steel
questions.solution: Chromium has the surface properties you want — it does not corrode, it resists scratches and it looks polished — but making the whole object from it would be expensive and it is not the ideal structural metal. So a thin chromium layer is electroplated onto iron or steel, which supplies the strength cheaply. This division of labour between the surface and the bulk is the reason electroplating exists.

questions.stem: When water is electrolysed, in what ratio by volume are hydrogen and oxygen produced?
questions.solution: Water is H₂O, so splitting it releases twice as many hydrogen molecules as oxygen molecules, and equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules. The ratio of hydrogen to oxygen by volume is therefore 2 : 1. Hydrogen collects at the cathode, the negative electrode, and oxygen at the anode. In the classic demonstration you can see it directly: the tube over one electrode fills twice as fast as the other, and the fuller one is hydrogen.

questions.stem: In electroplating an object with copper, what is used as the anode?
choices: A plate of pure copper, which dissolves to replace the copper leaving the solution
A carbon rod, which does not react
The object being plated itself
A strip of zinc
questions.solution: The anode is a plate of the same metal being deposited. As copper ions leave the solution and settle on the cathode, copper from the anode dissolves into the solution to replace them, so the concentration stays roughly constant and plating can continue steadily. The anode is gradually consumed and the object gains what it loses — the solution is really just the delivery route.

questions.stem: During the electrolysis of water, 6 mL of hydrogen is collected. What volume of oxygen is collected in the same time?
choices: 3 mL
12 mL
6 mL
1.5 mL
questions.solution: Hydrogen and oxygen come off in a 2 : 1 ratio by volume, so oxygen is half the hydrogen: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 mL. The trap is doubling instead of halving. Anchor it to the formula H₂O — the subscript 2 is on the hydrogen, so hydrogen is the gas there is more of.

questions.stem: Why are food cans coated with tin rather than with zinc?
choices: Tin is far less reactive than zinc, so it does not contaminate the food
Tin is a better conductor of electricity than zinc
Zinc cannot be electroplated onto iron
Tin is cheaper than zinc
questions.solution: Both metals protect the iron underneath from rusting, so on corrosion grounds either would do. The deciding factor is what touches the food: zinc is reactive enough to react with the contents and contaminate them, while tin is much less reactive and stays put. Zinc is used on objects that food never touches, such as galvanised buckets and roofing sheets.

questions.stem: During the electrolysis of water, a total of 24 mL of gas is collected from both electrodes together. What volume of oxygen is in that total?
choices: 8 mL
12 mL
16 mL
6 mL
questions.solution: The gases come off in a 2 : 1 ratio, so think of the total as being divided into 2 + 1 = 3 equal parts. Each part is 24 ÷ 3 = 8 mL. Oxygen is one part, so 8 mL, and hydrogen is two parts, 16 mL — and those add back to 24, which is the check worth doing. The common error is halving 24 to get 12, which would be the answer if the ratio were 1 : 1.

questions.stem: An LED is often preferred over a bulb when testing whether a liquid conducts. What property makes it the better choice, and what must be watched?
choices: It lights at a much smaller current, but it only works if its longer leg is connected towards the positive terminal
It lights at a much larger current, and it may be connected either way round
It produces more heat, which speeds up the reaction
It works only with alternating current
questions.solution: An LED glows at currents far below what a filament bulb needs, so it detects weak conduction that would otherwise be mistaken for none — the same reasoning that makes a compass needle a good detector. The catch is that an LED conducts in one direction only: its longer leg must go towards the positive terminal. Connected backwards it stays dark even when current would flow, which produces exactly the false negative the LED was brought in to prevent.
